To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in the adult GK rat, a genetic animal model of type II diabetes, β-cell regeneration is less efficient than that of the non-diabetic W rat, after 90% Px.

the adult hyperglycaemic GK rat is characterized by a low β-cell mass and a low proliferative capacity, both of which can be restored by 90% pan-creactomy, but to a lesser extent as compared to Wistar controls, suggesting that the GK rat is characterized both by an intrinsic defect in β-cell growth and an impaired response to β-cell stress.

in the Goto-Kaizaki (Gk) rat, a spontaneous genetic model of type II diabetes, there is an early restriction of the β cell mass that persists in the adult animal, and that this defect is the result of genetic predisposition contributing with an altered β-cell growth potential already present in neonatal period, as well as environmental factors (chronical hyperglycemia), leading to a reduced proliferative capacity specific for the adult animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the β-cell growth capacity and the mechanisms involved in its activation.
the study of the β-cell regenerative capacity in the adult GK rat, and the comparison with W rats, in order to better define the mechanisms involved in the β-cell regeneration process.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the β-cell regeneration in the adult GK rat is impaired.
the β-cell regeneration potential of the GK rat is impaired in the adult, as a consequence of both genetic predisposing factors and chronic hyperglycaemia.
in the adult GK rat the β-cell growth capacity is reduced as compared to the W rat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
β-cells are less able to proliferate, and to differentiate from ducts in the adult hyperinsulinemic GK rat as compared to the adult normoinsulinemic W rat.

in the adult GK rat, there is a reduced capacity to regenerate β-cells, and that this is due to a combination of factors, including the genetic background of the rat, and the presence of hyperglycemia.
in the GK rat, β-cell regeneration in response to a severe β-cell damage is less efficient as compared to the normal W rat, and this defect may contribute to the progression of the diabetic state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
β-cell neogenesis is not only impaired in the GK rat at birth and in the neonatal stage, but also in the adult hyper-glycemic state.
the adult hyperglycaemic GK rat is not a good animal model to study β-cell regeneration after Px.
in adult GK/Px rats the β-cell mass remains reduced, and the β-cell regeneration potential, although present, is lower than that of non-diabetic W/Px rats.
